stories.headline: Australia cricket captain describes Khawaja’s Sandpapergate claim as ’utter nonsense’
stories.deck: Australia captain Pat Cummins has rejected claims from ex-teammate Usman Khawaja about knowing of ball tampering plan in the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal
stories.bodyText:
Australia captain Pat Cummins has described as “utter nonsense” claims from ex-teammate Usman Khawaja that he knew about using sandpaper to tamper with a ball in a 2018 cheating scandal that rocked cricket.
Cummins held an extraordinary news conference Friday (November 13, 2026) to address allegations made in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, published this week, hours ahead of Australia's home-season opening one-day international against England in Perth.
Khawaja has said he published his account, which the whole team knew about, of the plot to support the three players who received unprecedented, lengthy bans from the sport as a result of the so-called Sandpapergate scandal.
He's had support from one of them — his longtime friend and fellow top-order batter David Warner, who posted on social media that the Cricket Australia investigation at the time was rushed and botched.
Cummins, who was part of the bowling attack in that test at Cape Town against South Africa, rejected it and accused Khawaja of being “casual” and “flippant” with his claims.
“When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he’s 100% wrong,” Cummins told a packed news conference in Sydney. “I’ve said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening.
“But I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper.
“That’s complete and utter nonsense.”
Cummins said he was prepared to answer questions all day if required, because he didn't want the topic to be dredged up again every time a book was published or another claim made.
After an hour, a cricket administrator suggested the news conference wind down, but Cummins again invited all questions to continue for as long as needed.
Steve Smith and Warner — the captain and vice-captain in that series eight years ago — were each banned for 12 months by Cricket Australia following an investigation into the cheating plot.
Cameron Bancroft, who was caught on TV footage using sandpaper on the ball during the test match, was banned for nine months.
Cricket Australia, team management and other players have rarely commented on the saga. The bowling group has rejected claims that everyone was in on the plot to use sandpaper to help make the ball “reverse” — or swing unconventionally through the air.
But in his autobiography, Khawaja said he was sitting beside Bancroft in the locker rooms at one stage and learned of a plot to tamper with the ball and urged caution.
Cummins on Friday turned the scenario back on Khawaja, who retired from the test team earlier this year.
“I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam to be careful when using sandpaper,” he said.
“That’s not the Usman that I know. It’s not the Usman that I think has been part of a team that’s helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years,” he said. “And the one that would have stopped that from happening there and then.”

briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: There were nine changes in the playing XIs as India and New Zealand made several changes for the fourth ODI of the five-match series at Mount Maunganui on Friday.
New Zealand made six changes, while India brought in three players. India captain 
Shreyas Iyer
 won the toss and elected to bowl first.
India are leading the series 2-0 after the third ODI in Hamilton was washed out due to rain.

As expected, India handed opportunities to Ruturaj Gaikwad, 
Ishan Kishan
 and 
Kuldeep Yadav
. Gaikwad will open the innings with Rohit Sharma after regular captain Shubman Gill was rested to prepare for the upcoming Test series.
Kishan replaced KL Rahul, who will also join the team's preparations for the two-match Test series.
Kuldeep Yadav was the third change in the Indian playing XI.
Speaking at the toss, Iyer said India wanted to make the most of the conditions and treat the remaining matches as important contests.
"We will bowl first," Iyer said.
Iyer said the possibility of dew later in the evening was one of the main reasons behind India's decision to bowl first.
"Yes, absolutely. I think it's about chasing, and when we looked at the wicket yesterday, there was a little bit amount of grass, but today it looks pretty dry, and also considering the dew coming in in the evening, one of the reasons we have opted to bowl first," Iyer said.
With India leading the series 2-0, Iyer said the team would treat the fourth and fifth ODIs as knockout games.
He also praised the team's approach despite the rain interruptions in the series.
"Well, it's important firstly to analyse the matches we've played before. So the coming two games, it's going to be crucial and of cardinal importance," Iyer said.

Obviously building the depth of our team leading into a World Cup year and then I guess them challenging themselves against a very, very good team," Santner said.
He also explained that the busy international schedule had played a role in the changes.
"With the schedules and stuff, I think India obviously had to do the same with the quick turnaround for the Test and then go to Australia. I think it's probably part of what we had to do. But yeah, it gives guys opportunities, which is nice."
Santner jokes about losing nine tosses in a row
"I think it's nine tails in a row. What were the odds on that? I won't be going to the casino anytime soon, but yeah, looks like a great day for cricket. It's usually a pretty good wicket here and obviously with the wind and a bit of sun, it'll be nice," Santner said.
"Yeah, it looks obviously a little bit of grass. I think it'll still have a bit of pace and bounce, but, I think with the wind and obviously the sun, it could dry out a little bit. But it should be a good wicket."

briefs.headline: What Cummins said about sandpaper scandal: Key points from explosive presser
briefs.deck: Pat Cummins rejected Usman Khawaja's claims that all players knew about the sandpaper during the 2018 scandal. He stated that Khawaja's assertions about a collective responsibility discussion were inaccurate and did not recall such a meeting. Cummins emphasized that there was no master-plan for ball-tampering and shared his thoughts on the severity of the players' punishments. He confirmed his…
briefs.bodyText:
Australia captain 
Pat Cummins
 has strongly rejected 
Usman Khawaja
's claims that the entire Australian team knew about the use of sandpaper during the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa.
Cummins addressed the allegations during a 68-minute press conference at Cricket Central in Sydney. He called Khawaja's claims "100% wrong" and "complete and utter nonsense".
Khawaja, in his recently published autobiography, alleged that the entire Australia XI knew about the use of sandpaper in the Cape Town Test. He also claimed that two players had refused to take collective responsibility for the incident.
Cummins responded to several allegations, spoke about the 2018 investigation, his relationship with Khawaja, the punishments handed to Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft, and his current relationship with Smith.
Key points from Pat Cummins' press conference
Did the entire Australian team know about the sandpaper?
Cummins strongly denied Khawaja's claim that all 11 players knew sandpaper was being used to tamper with the ball during the Cape Town Test in 2018.
"When he says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100% wrong," Cummins said. "I've said that consistently for the last eight years, I did not know that was happening.
"But I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense. I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper.
"That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that I think, or that has been part of a team that's helped rebuild this Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and you know the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then. Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations.
"In his book, Ussie has been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket.
"I support his right to tell a story 100%. I'm really glad that he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."
Was there a master-plan to tamper with the ball?
Cummins admitted that the Australian team had a win-at-all-costs mentality in 2018. He also spoke about an "ugly underbelly" and too many groups within the team. However, he rejected the suggestion that there was a planned effort to use illegal methods to make the ball reverse.
"There was no master-plan around using illegal methods," Cummins said. "I think that's maybe something that hasn't been spoken about enough. People assume you've gone from very legal methods [to get the ball to reverse] to suddenly taking sandpaper, and there must have been some huge master-plan.
"The truth, that is not the case.
"That's one of the reasons why I really want to talk through [it], because context and details matter around this. There's no grand plan. There's no team meeting. There's no bowlers saying this is what must happen. I think there's natural progressions that get you there."
Did Cummins know about sandpaper being used before the Port Elizabeth Test?
Khawaja also alleged that sandpaper had been used on the ball near the boundary before the start of a session during the Port Elizabeth Test, now known as Gqeberha. That match took place before the Cape Town Test.
Cummins said this was new information for him and that he was surprised by the claim.
"That was news to me this week," Cummins said. "I had no idea. Even chatting a couple of guys, that was a revelation to us. That was one of the things that really surprised me because that doesn't happen anymore.
"The umpires give the ball out to you in the middle, so I don't remember that. I remember growing up, used to watch for the umpire dropping the ball, but I genuinely don't remember that being the case. I don't know where that stopped. So that was a revelation to me this week."
Had Cummins ever seen ball-tampering during his career?
Cummins said the only time he had seen someone use an illegal object to change the condition of the ball was early in his career in a Sheffield Shield match.
He recalled a senior New South Wales batter using a bottle cap on the ball. However, he refused to reveal the player's name or the match.
"He was a batter," Cummins said. "He was a senior player, I won't mention him, but he took a bottle cap out in the field, and that was the one time I've seen on the field. I was looking at it going, 'Wow, that's not okay.' It was dealt with. The umpires knew it as well. They called him out and said, 'You've got to stop that right now.' He was dealt with. That's the only time I've seen something illegal out there."
Did two players refuse to take collective responsibility?
Khawaja claimed that he had asked the Australian team to take collective responsibility for the ball-tampering incident in Cape Town. He also alleged that two players had refused to support his suggestion.
Cummins said he did not remember any such discussion or team meeting.
"First part, I don't remember any conversation around collective responsibility," Cummins said. "I don't remember any team meeting where he stood up and said, 'Let's all own this as a team'. So then, to follow on, no, I've got no idea who those two people would be because I don't remember ever being asked or having a conversation about it.
"I've spoken to quite a few other people, and [they are] exactly the same. Trying to piece it all together, no one remembers a team meeting where someone stood up and said, 'We got to all own this.'"
Was Cummins interviewed during the original investigation?
Cummins confirmed that he was interviewed as part of Cricket Australia's investigation into the Cape Town incident.
The investigation was conducted by Cricket Australia's then-head of integrity Iain Roy and High Performance manager Pat Howard.
Cummins said the bowlers were among those specifically asked to take part. He added that other players were also given an opportunity to share information.
"I got asked to be part of that review," Cummins said. "There were some people that got specifically asked. I think it was the bowlers, and I can't really remember who else. And then I remember specifically a couple of times [them] saying, 'If anyone else has different accounts, or anyone else has information they'd like to share, please come forward and do that.' I did my interview. I was totally truthful. I've been very consistent since then at that event till now. Nothing's changed."
Why was Khawaja not interviewed in the investigation?
Khawaja alleged in his book that he was not interviewed during the original investigation, despite sitting next to Bancroft in the Cape Town dressing room.
Cummins said he had spoken to Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg before the press conference to confirm his recollection of the investigation.
"I actually even spoke to Todd today," Cummins said. "He's like, 'I've read all the investigations. Guys have been very, very consistent this whole time.'"
Should Cricket Australia reopen the investigation?
Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg had said earlier in the week that the governing body would not reopen the investigation.
When asked whether the investigation should be conducted again, Cummins said the decision was up to Cricket Australia.
"That's up to CA," Cummins said. "Part of why I think this is still lingering after eight years is there's a lot of context around this, which is hard to explain and hard to articulate, and that's what I want to do today. But there's a very proper way to do things and an improper [way], and I think that investigation was the proper way to do it. Everyone was asked in the circumstances, with a game very quickly after, so yeah, that's for CA. I think you could maybe argue whether the judgments were fair, but what can you do? I got asked all the questions, and answered them all fairly."
Has Cummins spoken to Khawaja? Will he take legal action?
Cummins confirmed that he had spoken to Khawaja during the week but did not reveal what they discussed.
He admitted that he was still trying to understand how the allegations would affect their long-standing friendship.
Cummins also said he had been advised that some of Khawaja's claims were "probably defamatory". However, he ruled out taking legal action.
"You've got to move on," he said. "It's been eight years … You got to draw the line at some point. I won't be doing that."
Why does Cummins feel Khawaja's claims are irresponsible?
Cummins spoke about his long friendship with Khawaja, who has been part of his cricket journey for 15 years.
However, he said the allegations were serious because they affected the lives and reputations of several people and their families.
"I've played 15 years, my debut for New South Wales and with Australia, Usman was right there, and he's been awesome to me, and he's a friend," Cummins said. "But this is people's real lives, and this is serious. I saw [my wife] Becky on the news yesterday. Like this affects not only people but people's families, and I'm one of the lesser ones. Maybe this week I'm right there. But talking eight years ago, like it was traumatic for those guys, for all of us, for Australian cricket, for fans. So to bring it up so flippantly and casually, I think it's irresponsible. So yeah, they're all things I'm grappling with at the moment."
Were the punishments handed to Smith, Warner and Bancroft too harsh?
Cummins made his position clear on the punishments given to Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft following the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.
He believed the bans handed to the three players were too severe.
Cummins also said he had not spoken to Warner or Bancroft since Khawaja's book was released. However, he said he had no issues with Bancroft, despite the batter's 2021 interview with The Guardian, in which he claimed it was "self-explanatory" that the bowling group knew about the sandpaper.
Cummins said the punishments were "way too heavy-handed" and "way over the top."
What is Cummins' relationship with Steve Smith now?
Cummins confirmed that he had spoken to Smith several times since the recent controversy.
Smith had withdrawn from the third Test in South Africa due to a neck injury. There had also been suggestions of frustration within the Australian camp following his withdrawal.
Cummins said their relationship was in a good place and that they were on the same page.
"I've spoken to Steve a few times since," Cummins said. "He's good. He's saying his neck is feeling better. I think he gets into Australia very soon, and I think he is due to play a Shield game soon.
"We're in a really good place. I think there was some unfair commentary around Steve in that last week. Perhaps I could have done a better job of trying to to soften that a bit. I think it probably got a little bit misconstrued how there was a level of disappointment in a such a big game that we were missing one of our great players. But no, we're very aligned going ahead. Very excited. He's very excited for the next 12 months. We'll need him. I'll need him, as captain, alongside me as vice-captain. So all very aligned."

briefs.headline: IND vs NZ 4th ODI: Auqib Nabi removes Dean Foxcroft; New Zealand 3 down vs India
briefs.bodyText:
Axar Patel to Finn Allen, Flat and short, on top of the off stump. Allen chops it down to cover.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, A little too straight, at the hips, on a nagging length. Young nudges it with soft hands through square leg. By the time the fielder in the deep can get in off the ropes, the batters come back for the run.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, Good energy behind the ball by Kuldeep. Wrong'un, on the shorter side, on middle. Young presses back to block but is squared up in defence. It squirts off the outer half towards backward point.
Tap to make your prediction
Kuldeep Yadav to Finn Allen, Looped up, on middle. Finn knocks it to long on and turns the strike over.
Kuldeep Yadav to Finn Allen, FOUR! Edged away. It is the googly by Kuldeep, not all that short, outside off. Allen flashes and flashes hard. The outside edge flies past Rohit Sharma before he can stick out his right hand.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, At 85 kph, flighted up, a bit of turn, on middle. Young plays it with the spin to the right of mid-wicket and gets to the other end.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, 150 up for New Zealand! Fullish delivery on the leg stump line, Young sinks to a knee and sweeps it to deep backward square leg for a couple of runs.
Spin is deployed from both ends now. Kuldeep Yadav (1-0-10-0) has a change of ends, and replaces Auqib Nabi. A slip in place in the form of Rohit.
Axar Patel to Finn Allen, This comes in with the arm, shorter and quicker, cramping Allen for room. One hand comes off the bat handle as Finn bunts it to mid-wicket.
The two umpires meet to inspect the ball, which appears to have gone out of shape. The fourth umpire rushes out with a box of replacement balls. Another one is selected and tossed back to Axar. Play is ready to resume.
Axar Patel to Finn Allen, SIX! Launched down the ground. Axar pushes the length up and tosses it up. Allen gets the ball right in the slot, and he also gets the width to free his arms. With a clean swing of the arms, he smokes it back over the sight screen for a maximum.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Slower and on a good length, outside off. Young punches it on the up through covers and crosses over.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Spears it in again, on a length. Will stabs it down the deck.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Fuller and angled in, on middle. Young defends by leaning forward.
Axar Patel to Will Young, FOUR! Good manipulation of the field. Bowled with a flatter trajectory, darted in on a good length, on middle. Young spots the gap behind square on the leg side. He reaches out in front and rolls his wrists over the ball to play the sweep well to the left of short fine leg.
Auqib Nabi to Will Young, Another short ball, aimed at the batter this time. Young gets his hands high and controls the pull down to deep square leg for a single.
Auqib Nabi to Will Young, Banged in short, getting it high around the shoulder. Young drops his hands and sways away to let the ball pass.
Auqib Nabi to Finn Allen, On a good length, on off. Allen knocks it off the back foot to cover, where Shreyas Iyer can't stay on his feet while trying to mop it up. It is parried away to his left, allowing the batters to cross over.
Auqib Nabi to Will Young, Into the deck but not all that short, on off. Young swivels for the pull but gets a bottom edge and it trickles down to deep fine leg for a run.
Auqib Nabi to Finn Allen, On the shorter side, on middle. Allen hops and drops it beside the strip on the leg side for a single.
Auqib Nabi to Finn Allen, FOUR! Easy pickings. Not the correct option, with square leg up inside the circle. This is dug into the surface, on off. This is not short enough to trouble the batter. Allen hangs back and plays the short-arm pull over square leg to pick up his first boundary.
Axar Patel to Finn Allen, Flighted up, on off. Allen strokes it through covers for another single.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Slows it down and tosses it up, on off. Young drives this full ball towards long off and rotates the strike.
Axar Patel to Finn Allen, Stays short, on off. Finn presses back and taps it to long on, getting off the mark with a single.
Axar Patel to Finn Allen, Shorter and on off. Allen punches it to wide mid off. Ishan Kishan, standing behind the stumps, is heard alerting Axar that Allen is playing from deep in his crease. A useful little observation from the keeper.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Sliding on with the arm, fractionally short. Young tickles it off the pads to the left of Naman Dhir at short fine leg for a run.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Full and drifting in at the off stump. Young leans across and hangs low to play the lap towards Naman Dhir at short fine leg.
Axar Patel comes back on, replacing Kuldeep Yadav.
Auqib Nabi to Finn Allen, Length-delivery on the stumps, Allen gently taps it to the leg side, just beside the pitch. A very successful over for Nabi upon his return. A wicket and just a single off it.
Auqib Nabi to Finn Allen, Beauty! Landed in and around off, on a length, Finn Allen gets squared up as he looks to defend. The ball straightens off the surface and zips past the outside edge. Beaten by a kitten-whisker.
Auqib Nabi to Finn Allen, Back of a length, at 133 kph, nipping away around off, Allen waits back and dabs it on the bounce to Rohit at first slip.
Finn Allen walks in next. Interestingly, this is the first time in his ODI career that Allen will be batting outside the opening position. Rohit Sharma is present at a wide slip for the new batter.
Auqib Nabi to Dean Foxcroft, OUT! CAUGHT IN THE DEEP! A reckless shot from Foxcroft and he throws his wicket away. Nabi bangs in a short delivery, following the batter. Foxcroft charges down the track to attack it with a hook, but the ball gets big on him and he loses his shape early, getting a top edge. The ball spoons high into the air and is safely taken by Gurnoor Brar at deep fine leg. New Zealand have slipped from 85/0 to 125/3.
Auqib Nabi to Will Young, A confident drive off the front foot and that will be FIFTY for Will Young! A fuller ball on middle stump, Young lets it come to him and pushes it to the left of Shreyas at cover for a single. He calmly raises his bat to acknowledge the applause from his teammates as he gets to his 13th ODI half-century. He looked a little scratchy early on and survived a couple of dropped chances, and will now look to convert this start into a big hundred.
Auqib Nabi to Will Young, Attacks the stumps and it skids a bit off a length, Young tucks it to mid on.
Another change in bowling as Auqib Nabi returns to the attack.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, Looped up, a bit too full, Will Young carves it to the left of Gaikwad at long off for a single. 10 runs off Kuldeep's first.
Kuldeep Yadav to Dean Foxcroft, Short outside off, turning in, Foxcroft rocks back and knocks it through mid off for a single.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, Spins in from off, on a length, Will hangs back and punches it to long on for a single.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, Shortens the length, does Yadav. Around off, Young punches it to the left of the bowler.
Kuldeep Yadav to Will Young, SIX! Top shot! A little bit of extra flight, full on the stumps, Young jumps down the track and hammers it down the ground for a six.
Kuldeep Yadav to Dean Foxcroft, Full ball on off, Dean pushes it to the left of mid off for a single. Gaikwad throws it to the bowling end, but it's wide of the target. The batters look to charge for the second, but the throw is backed up in the leg side. So they settle for a single only.
Playing his first game of the tour, Kuldeep Yadav has been introduced into the attack. He is starting with a slip in place.
Gurnoor Brar to Will Young, FOUR! No need to run for that! Another short delivery on the stumps, sitting up nicely for the batter. Will Young picks the length early and slaps it with a pull shot, wide of Rohit at mid-wicket for a cracking boundary. He moves to 41, does Young.
Gurnoor Brar to Will Young, Fantastic stop by Rohit! Saves a certain boundary there, as this was travelling at the rate of knots. A sharp short delivery by Brar on middle. Will Young nails the pull shot off the back foot, but Rohit Sharma dives to his right at mid-wicket and makes a half-stop, but the ball stays close to him.
Gurnoor Brar to Dean Foxcroft, Drop and run! Back of a length, nipping away off the seam, on off, Dean Foxcroft hangs back and taps it to the cover region and steals a quick single.
Gurnoor Brar to Will Young, Angled onto the pads, too full and Young clips it behind square on the leg side for a single.
Gurnoor Brar to Dean Foxcroft, On a good length, on the bodyline, Dean Foxcroft tucks it with soft hands between mid on and mid-wicket for a quick single. Auqib Nabi runs to his right, picks and throws in a motion towards the bowling end, but misses his shy.
Gurnoor Brar to Will Young, An attempted yorker, on off, Young jams the bat down, opens its face to guide it towards deep third for a single.
Axar Patel to Will Young, Tight on the stumps, a bit full around off, Young drives it to the extra cover region for a single.

briefs.headline: Ambekar, Gunjan script history with boxing gold medals at Youth Olympics
briefs.deck: Ambekar beat Ireland’s Kristen Jubani 3-2; Gunjan won 5-0 over Algeria’s Bouthaina Bensalah, becoming India’s first-ever woman to claim a boxing gold at the Youth Olympic Games
briefs.bodyText:
L. Ambekar Meetei and Gunjan scripted history by winning India's first couple of boxing gold medals at the Youth Olympic Games, defeating Ireland's Kristian Jubani and Algeria's Bouthaina Bensalah in their respective men's 50kg and women's 48kg finals here on Thursday.
First, Ambekar beat Jubani 3-2 to claim the top prize and create history. Soon after, Gunjan added to India's best-ever tally with a convincing 5-0 win over Bensalah, becoming the country's first-ever woman to claim a boxing gold at the Games.
Earlier, Ambekar's triumph marked a landmark moment for Indian boxing at the Youth Olympics, with Shiva Thapa's (60kg) silver medal at the 2010 Games being the country's previous best performance in the sport.
However, Gunjan soon joined Ambekar in the rare club following her victory. All five judges scored the bout in Gunjan's favour.
Vikas Krishan has a bronze to his name at the Youth Olympics Games, winning the medal in the 2010 edition in Singapore.
Ambekar, who trains at the National Institute of Sports (NIS) in Patiala, enjoyed a dominant run to the final, stopping Namibia's Abraham Kalenga in the first round of their quarterfinal bout before registering a comprehensive 5-0 victory over Colombia's Izzon Jeffrey Galea Arevalo in the semifinals.
Ambekar, from Manipur, then held his nerve in a closely contested final to prevail by a 3-2 split decision and secure the historic gold.
In her quarterfinal bout, Gunjan defeated Mexico's Atena Sofia Juarez Calero by a 5-0 unanimous decision to guarantee India a medal.
In the semifinal, Haryana's Gunjan beat Great Britain's Lily Bassett 4-1 in a hard-fought bout.
This is India's best performance at the Youth Olympics. PTI AH PDS AH KHS

briefs.headline: Vivaan Kapoor wins trap silver, secures India’s LA 2028 Olympic quota
briefs.deck: Vivaan became only the fourth Indian men’s trap shooter after the legendary Karni Singh (silver), Manavjit Singh Sandhu (gold) and Zorawar Singh Sandhu (bronze in 2025) to win a medal at the World Championships in the highly competitive discipline
briefs.bodyText:
India's Vivaan Kapoor came within touching distance of a world title before settling for silver in the men's trap event at the ISSF World Championships here on Thursday, but his podium finish also earned the country a quota place for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
The 24-year-old from Jaipur was in superb form and looked set to become only the second Indian to win a world title in men's trap after Manavjit Singh Sandhu, who triumphed at the 2006 World Championships in Zagreb, Croatia.
However, a miss in the shoot-off against Kuwait's Abdulrahman Alfaihan cost Vivaan the gold after both shooters finished the regulation 30-shot final tied at 29. Alfaihan held his nerve in the tie-break to claim the title.
Vivaan, though, became only the fourth Indian men's trap shooter after the legendary Karni Singh (silver), Manavjit Singh Sandhu (gold) and Zorawar Singh Sandhu (bronze in 2025) to win a medal at the World Championships in the highly competitive discipline.
Vivaan, whose best before this achievement had been a silver medal at the 2024 ISSF World Cup Final in New Delhi, also became the third Indian shooter after men's 10m air pistol marksman Jaypal Malviya and men's 50m rifle 3-positions bronze medallist Niraj Kumar to secure an LA 2028 Olympic quota place.
Vivaan had been remarkably consistent throughout the final, with his only miss coming on the 28th shot. Alfaihan, 40, a junior world champion in 2006 and a three-time Asian champion, had been trailing by a point before drawing level at 27-27 when the Indian missed his 28th shot. Both shooters then finished with 29 hits apiece, narrowly missing out on a perfect score of 30, which would have been a world record.
The shoot-off turned into a nerve-wracking contest, with both marksmen hitting their first two targets. But Vivaan missed the third, while the experienced Kuwaiti made no mistake and celebrated with his coach.
China's Qi Ying, the 2024 Paris Olympics silver medallist, took bronze, while Paris Olympics gold medallist Nathan Hales of Great Britain finished fifth.
India's second finalist, Udaivir Singh Jaiji, finished sixth after being eliminated following the first 15 shots, managing 11 hits. Having two Indian shooters in the final was itself a rare achievement.
Making his maiden senior World Championships final, Vivaan said his experience of competing against some of the world's leading shooters had helped him handle the pressure.
"I guess I just gave my best. I focused on my job like always. I've played against a couple of these shooters before, so that experience helped me and also a big thanks to (foreign coach) Peter (Wislosn) for training us before this competition," said Vivaan.
"It was lovely the way he trained us during the national camp and also to my personal coach Giovanni Cernogoraz... shooting with him is like shooting with the champions, so that made me also stronger and (to compete) against shooters of this level and then in the end I was just flowing in, just trying to do my job," he said.
On securing the Olympic quota for the country, Vivaan said: "I feel that it's a great thing that I could do for the country and I'm very happy that now we have a quota and let's hope I give my best and hope to shoot better and better."
The Indian trio of Vivaan, Udaivir and Zorawar finished fourth in the men's trap team event, missing out on bronze on a count-back after being tied on an aggregate score of 354 with Poland and the Czech Republic.
Kuwait clinched gold with a total of 356, while Poland and the Czech Republic took silver and bronze, respectively, both finishing on 354.
Earlier, in the three-day qualification round comprising five series of 25 shots each, Vivaan shot 120/125 to finish sixth after a tense shoot-off involving six other shooters who were all tied on the same score. Udaivir, who also shot 120/125, scraped into the final in eighth and last place after the shoot-off. Olympic champion Nathan Hales topped the qualification with 123, followed by Olympic silver medallist Qi Ying on 122.
The Indian women's trap team of Pragati Dubey (110/125), Manisha Keer (107) and Neeru Dhanda (105) finished seventh with an aggregate score of 322, while Italy clinched gold with 348. None of the three Indian shooters could make it to the eight-shooter individual final.

briefs.headline: Liam Lawson retains his F1 seat at Racing Bulls alongside Arvid Lindblad
briefs.deck: “We’re delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027. Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing,” team principal Alan Permane said
briefs.bodyText:
Liam Lawson is staying in Formula 1 for 2027 with Racing Bulls alongside teammate Arvid Lindblad after speculation he would be replaced by up-and-coming Formula 2 driver Nikola Tsolov.
Racing Bulls gave Tsolov a run in practice for last month’s Mexico City Grand Prix and has historically preferred to try out younger talent if its existing drivers didn’t make a permanent step up to the main Red Bull team. Instead, Tsolov gets a reserve driver role with Red Bull.
“We’re delighted to be continuing with Liam and Arvid for 2027. Both have demonstrated their ability and potential throughout the season, and we’ve seen the progress they’ve made, both individually and as a pairing,” team principal Alan Permane said on Thursday.
“I have no doubt that this is the best driver lineup for us, bringing a strong combination of experience and ambition. Together, we have a solid foundation to build on the progress made this year, continue pushing ourselves forward and take the next step towards achieving our ambitions in 2027.”
Lawson has outperformed his rookie teammate Lindblad this year and the New Zealander is ninth in the championship, in a year which has restored his reputation in F1 after a failed two-race stint with Red Bull in early 2025. Lindblad is 11th.
Lawson returned to Red Bull briefly with solid results in a three-race stand-in role when Isack Hadjar was sidelined by a wrist injury. Lawson said on Thursday that Racing Bulls was “building something super positive” ahead of 2027.
Tsolov is in second place in F2 with two rounds remaining and is aiming to become the first Bulgarian driver in F1 history.
